title: New creation (2 Corinthians 5:14–21)
hook: if anyone is in Christ, new creation; and the ministry of reconciliation is handed on
tomorrow: how do people with almost nothing give with joy?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: a house not made with hands, and a tent worth caring for. Today, what Paul says is new inside the tent.
screen: `A HOUSE NOT MADE WITH HANDS.` → `WHAT'S NEW INSIDE?`

segments.voice: Two people who used to be close spot each other in the cereal aisle, and both suddenly need to study the granola very carefully. Nobody wants to go first, because going first feels like losing. Paul has a word for undoing that kind of distance, and this chapter is full of it. The surprise is who he says went first.
screen: `THE CEREAL AISLE.` → `NOBODY WANTS TO GO FIRST.` → `WHO WENT FIRST?`

segments.voice: It starts with pressure: "For the love of Christ constraineth us." It presses on us, hems us in. Because of that, Paul says, "henceforth know we no man after the flesh." He stops sizing people up the old way. Then the line at the center: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." The King James says creature; the Greek word can also be read as creation, which is where the title comes from. Then the word of the day. "All things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation." Reconciliation means making peace again where a relationship was broken. And in Paul's telling, God doesn't wait at the far end of the aisle for an apology. "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." Not keeping score. That's who went first. Then the job is handed on: "we are ambassadors for Christ." An ambassador carries a message from one side to the other. Christians explain how this reconciling works in different ways, but here the new creation and the work of making peace arrive together. One to tell a friend: in Paul, going first isn't losing. It's the family resemblance.
screen: `THE LOVE OF CHRIST CONSTRAINETH.` · `A NEW CREATURE, ALL THINGS NEW.` · `GOD WENT FIRST, KEEPING NO SCORE.` · `AMBASSADORS: CARRY THE PEACE.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS NEW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've been dodging, in a hallway, a group chat, at a family table. If it's safe and right, draft one short, warm line to them, to send now or later; if that person hurt you, simply hold them in mind with as little score-keeping as you can. Distance can be wise, and peace doesn't always mean closeness.
Reconciliation. Making peace again where something was broken, and in Paul's telling, God goes first and hands the work on.
Keep this one: all things new, and it starts with whoever moves first. Peace to you.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate a sacrament of reconciliation or confession; other churches practice confession and making peace in other ways, and 2 Corinthians 5:17 is read at some baptisms.

notes: The index word is 'reconciliation' while the title is 'New creation'; the lesson teaches both and keeps the word exactly.
'The Greek word can also be read as creation' (κτίσις, 5:17) is a translation note; confirm. Trapdoor's gloss of καταλλαγή as 'a change from enmity to peace' follows standard lexicons; confirm.
'Christians explain how this reconciling works in different ways' stands in for theories of atonement, which the lesson does not name or rank.
'It's the family resemblance' is an application (God goes first; those reconciled are handed the same ministry, 5:18–20), not a quotation. Confirm.
The practice keeps a safety line: distance from someone who hurt you can be wise; reconciliation is not pressed on anyone.
